passage: Note for Payal's parents, Tuesday. At snack time a steel tray slid off the counter and crashed. Payal went stiff, eyes wide, then wailed and crawled straight into my lap. I held her and said, "Big bang. The tray fell. You're safe." She peeked at the tray, sniffed, and after a few minutes went back to her banana. From tomorrow I'll tell the children before we move the noisy trays. Maria 🙂

qa.q: What fell and crashed at snack time?
qa.a: A steel tray slid off the counter and crashed at snack time.

qa.q: What does Payal going stiff and crawling into Maria's lap suggest she felt?
qa.a: It suggests the sudden crash frightened her, and she went to Maria because she wanted to feel safe again.

qa.q: Which of Maria's choices helped Payal settle, and why?
qa.a: Holding Payal and naming the noise in simple words helped her calm down, and warning the children before moving trays can stop the shock from happening again.

qa.q: How might Payal's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They may feel reassured that Maria noticed Payal's fright and comforted her quickly. 😊

grounding: Shows a toddler's instinctive fear reaction to a sudden loud noise and a calm adult comforting her.

passage: The village fair was busy with bangle stalls and swings. Irawati rode on her Aaba Shankar's shoulders, clapping at the colours. Then a drummer beside the temple steps started beating hard without warning. Irawati jerked, grabbed two fistfuls of Shankar's hair and let out a thin cry. Shankar lifted her down and held her against his chest, walking to the quiet side of the pond. She kept her face hidden for a while, then slowly turned to watch the drummer from far away.

qa.q: Where did Shankar carry Irawati after the drumming started?
qa.a: He carried her to the quiet side of the pond.

qa.q: Why did Irawati grab Shankar's hair and cry out?
qa.a: The drumming began suddenly and loudly, so she was startled and scared, and she held on to the person she felt safest with.

qa.q: What did Shankar do that suited a frightened toddler?
qa.a: He moved her away from the noise and held her close without hurrying her, letting her look again only when she was ready.

qa.q: What would change if Shankar had stayed near the drummer and told her not to cry?
qa.a: Irawati would likely have stayed frightened and cried harder, because the loud sound would keep hitting her and her fear would not be comforted.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler's instinctive fear of a sudden loud noise in a crowded, unfamiliar place.

passage: On a windy Saturday in a park in Cape Town, Daniel toddled after a rolling ball while his father Thabo sat on the grass. A large brown dog came bounding out from behind a bench. Daniel stopped dead, threw his arms up and screamed, then ran back and clung to Thabo's leg. Thabo scooped him up and asked the owner to call the dog. From his father's arms, Daniel watched the dog sit, his fingers still gripping Thabo's shirt.

qa.q: What came out from behind the bench?
qa.a: A large brown dog came bounding out from behind a bench.

qa.q: What does Daniel's grip on Thabo's shirt show about how he felt, even after the dog sat?
qa.a: It shows he still felt uneasy and wanted to stay close to his father, because the dog had appeared so suddenly.

qa.q: How could Thabo help Daniel feel calmer around dogs over time?
qa.a: He could let Daniel watch calm dogs from a safe distance in his arms, and never push him to touch one before he is ready.

qa.q: How might the dog's owner see Daniel's scream?
qa.a: The owner might think the dog was only being playful, but could also understand that a big dog rushing up is scary for a small child.

grounding: Shows a toddler's instinctive fear reaction to a sudden movement by a large dog.

passage: I was hanging clothes on my balcony when the construction crane next door dropped a steel pipe. Clang! Across the gap, little Akash, who is maybe two, froze on his mat, arms flung wide. Then he scrambled backwards on his bottom, bumped into his mother's knees and buried his face in her dupatta. He did not look up again until the workers went quiet. Sonali, his mother, just held him and rocked.

qa.q: What sound made Akash freeze on his mat?
qa.a: A steel pipe dropped by the construction crane next door made a loud clang.

qa.q: What does Akash hiding his face in the dupatta suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He was probably frightened by the sudden noise and wanted the safety of his mother, though the neighbour can only guess from what she saw.

qa.q: What could Sonali do if the building noise keeps startling Akash?
qa.a: She could keep holding him close when loud bangs come, and later name the sound calmly, like 'that was the big pipe', so it feels less strange.

qa.q: How does the neighbour see Akash's reaction?
qa.a: She sees it as a quick, natural startle and notices how fast his mother's rocking settled him.

grounding: Illustrates an instinctive fear reaction in a toddler to a sudden loud noise, seen by a neighbour.

passage:
Monday: Abba switched on the mixer grinder and Zainab screamed, dropped her spoon and ran to the bedroom door, sobbing.
Thursday: Anand, her Abba, held her in the kitchen doorway before switching it on. She pressed her hands over her ears and hid her face in his shirt, but stayed.
The next week, she heard the lid click, covered her ears herself, and watched the chutney whirl from his lap.

qa.q: Where did Zainab run the first time the mixer grinder started?
qa.a: She ran to the bedroom door, sobbing.

qa.q: Why did Zainab scream and run on Monday?
qa.a: The sudden roar of the mixer grinder scared her; her body reacted before she could understand what the noise was.

qa.q: What worked well in how Anand helped her?
qa.a: He did not force her close; he held her at a safe distance and warned her by his presence, so she could get used to the noise bit by bit.

qa.q: What would change if Anand had laughed at her fear or made her stand near the grinder?
qa.a: She might have grown more scared of the kitchen, because her fear would have been pushed instead of calmed. 😟

grounding: Shows a toddler's instinctive fear of a loud machine easing over several days with a caregiver's support.
